title: Discrete-Time Signal Processing, MIT 6.341, Fall 2005 — shard 3: Lectures 17–23, Problem Sets 9–11, Projects I–II, and Fall 2005 final
access: Full assigned MIT-published corpus read from the official MIT OpenCourseWare course package at https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-341-discrete-time-signal-processing-fall-2005/6.341-fall-2005.zip. The shard contains six posted lecture-note PDFs (Lectures 17–22); Lecture 23, ‘Caruso’s Orchestra,’ is listed on the schedule but has no posted notes. Problem Sets 9–11 and their solutions, the combined Projects I–II instructions and supporting MAT/WAV/MATLAB files, and the Fall 2005 final with its solution were all read or inspected. The final solution is a handwritten image scan and was OCRed, with exact notation checked against the scan where needed. The OCW course page links CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 terms, subject to third-party-content exceptions; the Lecture 21 speech waveform is explicitly reproduced from another Oppenheim volume and was not retained as an image candidate.
topics: Lecture 17, p. 1 — Spectral-analysis chain for continuous-time signals: anti-alias filtering, sampling and frequency normalization, finite-duration windowing, and DFT sampling.
Lecture 17, pp. 1–2 — Windowing as periodic frequency-domain convolution; main-lobe smearing, sidelobe leakage, Kaiser-window shape/length tradeoffs, and computational cost.

Lecture 17, pp. 2–3 — Spectral sampling, the picket-fence illusion, finite-record versus periodic-signal interpretations, zero padding as denser sampling rather than improved resolution, and window-length control of resolvability.
Lecture 18, pp. 1–2 — Three spectral-analysis illusions; PSD applications in system identification and noise removal; periodogram definition and its autocorrelation interpretation.
Lecture 18, pp. 3–4 — Periodogram mean, bias, asymptotic unbiasedness, nonvanishing variance, and failure of consistency.

Lecture 18, pp. 4–7 — Averaged periodograms, variance reduction, record-length allocation between segment count and window length, overlap, Hamming windows, and bias–variance/resolution–smoothness tradeoffs.
Lecture 19, pp. 1–2 — Direct DFT cost, limits of small constant-factor shortcuts, composite-size FFT factorization, and radix-2 complexity.
Lecture 19, pp. 2–3 — Radix-2 decimation-in-frequency: even/odd frequency subsequences, time aliasing, recursive butterflies, operation counts, and bit-reversed output.

Lecture 19, pp. 3–4 — Radix-2 decimation-in-time: even/odd input subsequences, butterfly simplification, bit-reversed input, transposed DIF/DIT flow graphs, in-place computation, and regular-memory alternatives.
Lecture 20, p. 1 — Algorithm selection by requested output: why computing one DFT bin directly can beat computing a full FFT.

Lecture 20, pp. 1–3 — Goertzel algorithm derived by expressing one DFT coefficient as a sampled output of a recursive LTI filter; real second-order realization, operation count, and arbitrary-frequency evaluation.

Lecture 20, pp. 3–4 — Chirp transform for uniformly spaced DTFT samples on an arbitrary arc of the unit circle; chirp modulation, convolution implementation, finite-record realizability, and adjustable starting frequency.
Lecture 21, pp. 1–2 — Motivation for time-local spectra from speech and music; time-dependent/short-time Fourier transform, spectrograms, chirp example, and window effects.

Lecture 21, pp. 3–5 — Frequency- and time-sampled STFT, reconstruction conditions, time–frequency resolution, modulated-filter-bank realization, downsampling of redundant time samples, and speech analysis.

Lecture 22, pp. 1–3 — Polyphase decomposition of a modulated filter bank, shared input polyphase components, transfer-matrix form, channel/output-rate accounting, and an R-fold saving over direct filtering.
Lecture 22, pp. 4–6 — Critically sampled modulated filter banks, DFT/FFT realization, total multiplication cost, and the special cases L=N=R and L=2N=2R with time aliasing.
Lecture 23 — ‘Caruso’s Orchestra’ is present in the OCW meeting sequence but has no posted lecture-note PDF or other shard artifact to summarize.

Problem Set 9 and solution, pp. 1–12 — DFT spectral analysis: CT/DT frequency calibration, window leakage and resolution, exact-bin effects, frequency zooming, periodogram/autocorrelation relationships, and diagnosis of periodogram, Welch, and all-pole estimates.

Problem Set 10 and solution, assignment pp. 1–6 and solution pp. 1–5 — STFT and modulated-filter-bank equivalences, arbitrary-radius z-transform sampling, multiplication-rate optimization, sampled analysis systems, and alias-canceling perfect reconstruction.

Problem Set 11 and solution, assignment pp. 1–3 and solution pp. 1–7 — Magnitude/phase constraints, Hilbert transforms, analytic signals and 90-degree phase splitters, complex cepstra, echo models, minimum-phase causal cepstral recursion, and time reversal.

Projects I–II, pp. 1–7 — Empirical phase audibility with all-pass speech filtering; comparative IIR/FIR speech denoiser design; specification normalization; numerical stability via second-order sections; decimation-aware polyphase design under a hardware multiplication budget; subjective evaluation on individualized utterances.
Project support corpus — projIA.mat speech/all-pass data, projIB.mat noisy-speech data, 52 mono 44.1-kHz Project II WAV utterances, and historical Athena/Sun MATLAB playback helpers.

Fall 2005 final and solution, exam pp. 1–24 and solution scan pp. 1–26 — Nine integrative problems spanning causal sequence recovery from Fourier parts, analytic-signal filtering, mixed CT/DT resampling, multirate identities, Parks–McClellan uniqueness, DFT samples via time aliasing, spectrum interpretation, correlation by DFT, filter-bank/DFT equivalence, and single-frequency evaluation by recursion.
key_results: For v[n]=x[n]w[n], windowing gives V(e^jω)=(1/2π)∫X(e^jθ)W(e^j(ω−θ))dθ: multiplication by a finite window becomes periodic convolution and smooths peaks and discontinuities. [Lecture 17 p. 1]

After sampling with period T and taking an N-point DFT, bin k corresponds to continuous-time angular frequency Ω_k=2πk/(NT), provided the anti-aliasing and CT/DT mapping assumptions hold. [Lecture 17 p. 1]

A window’s main-lobe width controls spectral smearing/resolution while sidelobe height controls leakage. Raising Kaiser β widens the main lobe and lowers sidelobes; at fixed β, increasing length narrows the main lobe and lowers sidelobes at the cost of a longer DFT. [Lecture 17 p. 2]

Zero padding a fixed record samples the same DTFT more densely and can reveal picket-fence behavior, but it does not improve the ability to resolve nearby components; resolution changes only when the record/window itself changes. [Lecture 17 pp. 2–3]
For a length-L rectangularly windowed record v[n], the periodogram is I(ω)=(1/L)|V(e^jω)|², equivalently the DTFT of the finite-record autocorrelation scaled by 1/L. [Lecture 18 pp. 2–3]

The periodogram mean is the true PSD convolved with the spectral window: E{I(ω)}=(1/L)P_xx(ω)*|W(e^jω)|². It is biased for finite L but asymptotically unbiased as the normalized spectral window approaches an impulse. [Lecture 18 pp. 3–4]

Increasing periodogram record length does not force its variance to zero: var{I(ω)}≈P_xx²(ω), so the raw periodogram is not a consistent PSD estimator even though its bias vanishes asymptotically. [Lecture 18 p. 4]

Averaging K approximately independent periodograms preserves the individual estimate’s mean while reducing variance by 1/K. For a fixed total record Q=KL, more segments produce a smoother but lower-resolution estimate because each window is shorter. [Lecture 18 pp. 4–5]

Half-window overlap can nearly halve the variance relative to nonoverlapping sections for the example discussed, while a tapered window changes the associated bias/leakage behavior. [Lecture 18 pp. 6–7]

Direct computation of an N-point complex DFT requires on the order of N² complex multiplications and additions; factorizing N=p1p2…pv yields FFT work proportional to N(p1+…+pv), and radix-2 reduces this to order N log2N. [Lecture 19 pp. 1–2]

In radix-2 DIF, even frequency samples are the N/2-point DFT of x[n]+x[n+N/2], while odd samples are the N/2-point DFT of (x[n]−x[n+N/2])W_N^n. Full recursion uses (N/2)log2N complex multiplications and Nlog2N complex additions. [Lecture 19 pp. 2–3]

In radix-2 DIT, X[k]=G[k]+W_N^kH[k], where G and H are N/2-point DFTs of the even- and odd-indexed input samples. The standard flow graph has bit-reversed input and normal output; node rearrangement can exchange normal and bit-reversed ordering. [Lecture 19 pp. 3–4]

A DIF flow graph can be obtained by transposing a corresponding DIT flow graph—swap input/output and reverse every edge—linking algorithm variants through the general transposition principle. [Lecture 19 p. 4]

To compute just one coefficient X[k] of an 8-point DFT, the canonical sum needs eight complex products and can be cheaper than running a full radix-2 FFT that produces all eight coefficients. [Lecture 20 p. 1]

The Goertzel derivation uses h[n]=W_N^(−kn)u[n): filtering x[n] and reading y_k[N] gives X[k]. Factoring the pole pair gives denominator 1−2cos(2πk/N)z^−1+z^−2 and a final complex numerator operation. [Lecture 20 pp. 1–3]

For one frequency, Goertzel requires N real multiplications plus one complex multiplication in the handout’s accounting, and the same recurrence can evaluate X(e^jω) at non-bin frequencies. [Lecture 20 p. 3]

The chirp transform rewrites uniformly spaced samples X(e^j(ω0+kΔω)) as pre-modulation by one chirp, convolution with a fixed conjugate chirp, and post-modulation. Finite support makes the otherwise noncausal/unstable-looking convolution implementable by bookkeeping. [Lecture 20 pp. 3–4]
The STFT/TDFT convention in the notes is X[n,λ)=Σ_m x[n+m]w[m]e^(−jλm); time advances by sliding x past a fixed window. A magnitude plot over n and λ is a spectrogram. [Lecture 21 pp. 1–2]

For fixed n, the STFT is the frequency-domain convolution of the shifted signal spectrum with W: X[n,λ)=(1/2π)∫e^(jθn)X(e^jθ)W(e^j(λ−θ))dθ, so the usual leakage–resolution window tradeoff remains local in time. [Lecture 21 p. 2]

Sampling the STFT at N frequencies produces the N-point DFT of the windowed block. For a length-L window and time hop R, the notes give exact-reconstruction feasibility when R≤L≤N; longer windows favor frequency resolution and shorter windows favor time resolution. [Lecture 21 p. 3]

A bank of modulated prototype filters h_k[n]=e^(jω_kn)h_0[n], with w[m]=h_0[−m], produces sampled STFT channels y_k[n]=X[n,λ)|_(λ=ω_k); downsampling each channel by R removes time redundancy. [Lecture 21 pp. 3–4]

Polyphase decomposition lets all N modulated filter branches share the R input polyphase components. Relative to direct LN complex multiplies per input sample, the polyphase form requires LN/R. [Lecture 22 pp. 1–4]

At critical sampling R=N, the modulated polyphase combination is an N-point DFT across the filtered polyphase signals and can be implemented by an FFT. The stated total cost is L/N+log2N multiplications per input sample. [Lecture 22 pp. 4–5]
When L=N=R, each prototype polyphase component is one tap; when L=2N=2R, each has two taps and the notes explicitly identify time aliasing in the N-point FFT representation. [Lecture 22 pp. 5–6]

With 8-kHz sampling, requesting CT frequency samples no farther than 5 Hz apart requires N≥1600; a 1000-sample record must therefore be zero-padded, though this improves grid spacing rather than window-limited resolution. [PS9 solution, Problem 9.1, p. 1]

Multiplying selected DFT bins by an ideal-looking binary mask does not implement ideal DTFT low-pass filtering between those bins. Subsequent decimation can alias the unconstrained inter-bin spectrum even when the retained DFT samples look correct. [PS9 solution, Problem 9.3, pp. 2–5]

For a windowed complex sinusoid, the largest-bin estimate has worst-case angular-frequency error π/(NT). Generalized-linear-phase information can refine it via ω0=ω_hat+2∠X_w[k_hat]/(M−1), under the main-lobe/sign conditions developed in the solution. [PS9 solution, Problem 9.4, pp. 6–7]

The IDFT of N evenly spaced periodogram samples is a periodically aliased version of the aperiodic record autocorrelation. For a length-L segment, N≥2L−1 prevents overlap and makes the sampled-spectrum and continuous-periodogram autocorrelation expectations agree over the supported lags. [PS9 solution, Problem 9.6, pp. 10–12]

In the PS9 estimator-identification exercise, main-lobe width reveals actual segment length, sample density reveals zero padding, variance reveals averaging, and the number of extrema distinguishes low- versus higher-order all-pole models. [PS9 solution, Problem 9.7, p. 12]
A modulated filter bank and a DFT of x[n]w[n] agree at time zero when the analysis window is the time reversal of the prototype: w[n]=h_0[−n]. [PS10 solution, Problem 10.1, p. 1]

Samples of a 256-point windowed z-transform on radius 0.9 can be produced by a causal modulated filter bank using h_0[n]=0.9^(n−256) for 1≤n≤256, modulation ω_k=−2πk/256, and output sample N_k=256. [PS10 solution, Problem 10.2, p. 2]

For the analyzed modulated filter bank, perfect reconstruction requires the desired (l=0) channel sum to equal R and every l=1,…,R−1 alias-component channel sum to vanish for all ω. [PS10 solution, Problem 10.4(d), pp. 4–5]

The discrete-time Hilbert transformer has response −j on 0<ω<π and +j on −π<ω<0; it maps cos(ω0n) to sin(ω0n), sin(ω0n) to −cos(ω0n), and an ideal lowpass sinc to (1−cos(ω_cn))/(πn). [PS11 solution, Problem 11.3, pp. 2–3]

Two all-pass branches whose phases differ by ±π/2 form a 90-degree splitter: w[n]=y1[n]+jy2[n] has zero negative-frequency spectrum and magnitude 2|X(e^jω)| over positive frequencies. [PS11 solution, Problem 11.4, pp. 3–4]
For an echo h[n]=δ[n]+αδ[n−n0], |α|<1, the complex cepstrum is an impulse train h_hat[n]=Σ_(k≥1)(−1)^(k+1)α^kδ[n−kn0]/k. [PS11 solution, Problem 11.5, pp. 4–5]

For a minimum-phase sequence, both x[n] and its complex cepstrum are causal. The cepstrum starts with x_hat[0]=log x[0] and the supplied convolution identity yields a causal recursion in which x_hat[n] depends only on x[0…n] and earlier cepstral samples. [PS11 solution, Problem 11.6, pp. 5–6]

For a real sequence, log-magnitude is even and unwrapped phase is odd, so the complex log spectrum is conjugate symmetric and the complex cepstrum is real; time reversal of x reverses its complex cepstrum. [PS11 solution, Problem 11.7, pp. 6–7]

The project warns that severe IIR specifications can place many poles near z=1, making direct-form coefficient quantization unstable even in floating point; pairing poles and zeros into stable second-order sections and cascading them is the prescribed workaround. [Projects handout p. 5]

Project II fixes the input rate at 44.1 kHz, appends decimation by four to 11.025 kHz, and limits the design to 17 multiplications per input sample; polyphase cost must be compared with high-rate direct cost for six IIR/FIR families. [Projects handout pp. 5–7]

The final’s DFT/correlation problem reinforces that IDFT{|X_N[k]|²} is a circularly aliased autocorrelation: the full autocorrelation of a 1024-sample record needs N≥2047, while lags |m|≤10 can be recovered already at the allowed minimum N=1024 by taking the corresponding head/tail circular indices. [Final exam Problem 7 pp. 20–21; solution scan pp. 22–23]

A first-order recursion y[n]=x[n]+ay[n−1] can evaluate one DTFT frequency: choosing a=e^(j2π/60) and sampling at any multiple of 60 greater than 89—e.g. M=120—makes y[M]=X(e^jω)|_(ω=2π/60) for a 90-sample input. [Final exam Problem 9 p. 24; solution scan p. 26]
pedagogy: This shard is organized around misconceptions, implementation choices, and diagnostic evidence. Lectures 17–18 repeatedly contrast what a DFT plot seems to say with what the finite record and window actually justify; the memorable ‘three illusions’ become a checklist for separating bin spacing, true resolution, bias, and variance. Lectures 19–20 derive algorithms from algebraic decompositions but insist that computational efficiency depends on the requested output: full FFTs, one-bin Goertzel evaluation, and arbitrary-arc chirp transforms solve different problems. Lectures 21–22 then close a long conceptual loop by deriving the STFT as both sliding-window DFT and modulated filter bank, exposing its polyphase and FFT structure and counting operations at each stage. Problem sets are compact but graduate-level: many textbook problems are referenced by number, while custom problems ask students to reverse-engineer spectra, recognize estimator fingerprints, prove equivalence or perfect reconstruction, and move among DTFT, DFT, z-transform, filter-bank, and multirate views. Solutions are unusually explanatory and often identify tempting wrong arguments. The projects are empirical design studies rather than canned calculations: students listen, compare six filter families, confront software conventions and numerical instability, account for multiplies, and explain subjective artifacts without submitting code. The final rewards concise reasoning rather than answer-only work and revisits earlier course material through novel system-identification and counterexample tasks. Prerequisites are mature discrete-time systems, DTFT/DFT and z-transform fluency, multirate identities, random-process spectra, filter design, complex variables, and MATLAB-style experimentation.

gems: The shard opens spectral analysis with a trap: a 64-bin DFT can show two perfectly clean lines while the finite record’s DTFT has energy almost everywhere and happens to be zero at every sampled in-between bin. [Lecture 17 pp. 2–3]

‘Three illusions’ compress the unit into a durable diagnostic: invisible between bins does not mean absent; denser zero padding does not mean better resolution; and more random-process data does not make one raw periodogram converge. [Lecture 18 p. 1]
White-noise periodograms from L=16 through L=1024 keep fluctuating around the flat truth, making inconsistency visible rather than merely algebraic. [Lecture 18 p. 4]

The fixed-data-record example makes estimator design a resource allocation problem: spend samples on longer windows for sharper peaks or on more segments for lower variance—you cannot maximize both. [Lecture 18 pp. 5–7]

For N=1024, the notes contrast roughly 10^6 direct DFT operations with roughly 10^4 radix-2 FFT operations, turning the asymptotic gain into an immediately memorable two-order-of-magnitude example. [Lecture 19 p. 2]
Lecture 20 begins with an algorithm-selection ambush: asking only for X[5] of an 8-point DFT makes the celebrated FFT a needlessly expensive choice. [Lecture 20 p. 1]

The chirp transform is presented not as a historical curiosity but as a hardware-friendly way to move an analysis arc around the unit circle while reusing one fixed convolution block. [Lecture 20 p. 4]
A speech fragment—‘should we chase …’—motivates why one global spectrum is the wrong object for speech; spectral locality changes with sound class over time. [Lecture 21 p. 1]

The final two posted lectures make three representations click into one object: sliding-window DFT samples, outputs of a modulated filter bank, and an FFT across filtered polyphase components. [Lectures 21–22]

PS9 makes students identify estimators from their visual fingerprints rather than from formulas: zero padding changes dot density, averaging changes roughness, segment length changes peak width, and model order changes the count of extrema. [PS9 Problem 9.7; solution p. 12]

A plausible ‘ideal lowpass’ made by zeroing DFT bins is dismantled carefully: it constrains only the samples and can leave enough stopband energy between them to alias after downsampling. [PS9 solution Problem 9.3, pp. 2–5]

Problem Set 11 is officially ‘Due: Never’ but the handout immediately says the final assumes it has been done—a compact bit of course culture attached to serious Hilbert/cepstrum material. [PS11 p. 1]
The echo model h[n]=δ[n]+αδ[n−n0] becomes an infinite, regularly spaced cepstral impulse train, a clean demonstration of why echoes are conspicuous in quefrency. [PS11 solution Problem 11.5, pp. 4–5]

Project I directly tests the folk theorem that the ear is insensitive to phase by comparing N=1 and N=50 all-pass speech filters and asking students to describe what they actually hear. [Projects handout pp. 2–3]

The denoising project compares Butterworth, both Chebyshev types, elliptic, Parks–McClellan, and Kaiser designs under identical audible-speech goals, forcing theoretical response differences into pole-zero, impulse, group-delay, cost, and listening evidence. [Projects handout pp. 4–5]
The hardware story gives the computational constraint personality: only 17 multipliers are available because the 18th is already committed to digital volume control. [Projects handout p. 6]

Project II’s 52 individualized noisy utterances turn a common filter-design assignment into a small blind listening investigation: each student must denoise their own file and discover what it says. [Projects handout p. 7; project2.zip]
The course refuses code-dump grading: project reports summarize method and plots, explicitly exclude MATLAB code, and use the EGRMU scale to judge understanding and effort. [Projects handout pp. 1–2]

The final casts Parks–McClellan uniqueness as a treasure-chest dispute: two entrants use different declared N values yet produce the same response, and students must reconcile that with the alternation theorem. [Final Problem 4 pp. 12–15; solution scan pp. 14–16]

The scanned final solution is itself evidence of the assessment philosophy: it contains a fully worked 100-point exam graded 98 under EGRMU-style marks, with reasoning written directly into the booklet rather than an answer key alone. [Final solution scan pp. 3–26]
